newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu's new promises said to cost billions.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu's new promises said to cost billions.

text.p: Written promises Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu gave coalition partners to defuse government crises will cost the Treasury up to three billion shekels ($841.7 million), Israeli newspapers said on Wednesday.

The agreements reached in the last month with Foreign Minister David Levy's Gesher faction and the Israel ba'Aliya immigrant party call for increased spending on education and a series of social causes.

Treasury officials, commenting on the agreements, said they had not seen the documents and could not estimate their cost but added that any additional expenditure would have to be offset by cuts elsewhere.
"Any additional funds...must come by cutting other clauses in the state budget," Finance Ministry director-general Shmuel Slavin told Reuters.
The daily Haaretz newsaper estimated the agreements would require additional spending of one to two billion shekels.
The Yedioth Ahronoth daily put the figure at three billion shekels. The reports coincided with parliament's approval of Yaacov Neeman as Netanyahu's new finance chief on Wednesday.
"What I can say, and I'll say this to the new finance minister Yaacov Neeman, is that there is certainly no money in the budget to finance such an agreement," Slavin said.
The prime minsiter's office said the cost of the agreements was unclear. "We're checking the cost but some of these expenditures have already been budgeted," a spokesman said.
Levy threatened last week to bolt Netanyahu's splintered coalition, charging the prime minister had violated promises and usurped his responsibilities in diplomacy and peacemaking.
Netnayahu resolved the tiff by signing an agreement outlining Levy's duties and promising to increase social spending.
The prime minister made other spending promises last month to appease coalition partner Israel ba'Aliya, prompting concern among financial analysts.
"Fiscal restraint is the key issue for the whole economy and the capital markets," said Victor Shohet, chief economist at Ofek Securities.
Analysts estimated a 3.5 billion to 4.0 billion shekel cut is needed in the 1998 budget to reduce inflationary pressures and revive sustainable growth.

Yoram Gabbay, a former Treasury revenues director and now a fund manager, said he doubted any finance minister will have much room to act on tightening the budget given the demands of Netanyahu's fractious coalition.
The government's large budget deficit in June prompted the Bank of Israel to call for immediate spending cuts.
Neeman, a prominent lawyer who served in the early 1980s as Finance Ministry director-general, is an outside appointment who belongs to none of the parties in Netanyahu's coalition.
He was appointed after Netanyahu's rival Dan Meridor resigned last month in a power struggle with the prime minister over foreign exchange policy.

"The new minister will have to be very strong. He will have to get the complete backing of the prime minister because he's an outsider, he's not a politician. If not, he will be swamped by politicians," Shohet said.
